blocks.text: After a thyroid operation a woman wakes with a hoarse, weak voice, and in the next bay a trauma patient has a drain placed into the chest through a neat opening under the armpit. Both operators were guided by anatomy: one by a nerve that hugs the thyroid, the other by a triangle that keeps the needle away from muscle, breast and abdomen.

blocks.markdown: The thoracic cage protects the heart and lungs, so surgeons gain access either through the **ribs** or through the **sternum**. In both approaches the layers are crossed from superficial to deep, and the neurovascular structures that run with the ribs must be avoided.

blocks.title: Intercostal neurovascular bundle
blocks.text: Each intercostal space contains the intercostal vein, artery and nerve (VAN from superior to inferior) running in the subcostal groove on the underside of the rib above. The bundle lies between the internal intercostal and innermost intercostal muscles.

blocks.markdown: **Thoracotomy** is an incision through an intercostal space. A common posterolateral thoracotomy in the fifth space crosses: skin; subcutaneous tissue; latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior, which are divided or retracted; the external intercostal, internal intercostal and innermost intercostal muscles; the endothoracic fascia; and the parietal pleura. The incision is made along the **upper border of the rib below** so that the bundle, which hides under the lower margin of the rib above, is protected.

items: Latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior (divided or retracted)

blocks.markdown: **Median sternotomy** is a longitudinal split of the sternum in the midline, used for heart surgery. The layers are skin, subcutaneous tissue, the pectoral fascia and periosteum on the front of the sternum, then the manubrium and body of the sternum, which are divided with a saw. Deep to the sternum lie the thymic remnant and fat, then the pericardium. Staying in the midline avoids the **internal thoracic vessels**, which run about a centimetre or two lateral to the sternal edge, and the pleural sacs, which are pushed away laterally.

rows: Latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior (and intercostals)
blocks.caption: Comparing two chest incisions.

blocks.title: Layers in a median sternotomy
blocks.prompt: A surgeon plans a sternotomy to reach the pericardium. List what is crossed and what should be avoided by staying in the midline.

steps.text: Skin and subcutaneous tissue are incised over the sternum.
The pectoral fascia and periosteum are divided and the bone is exposed.
The sternum is split longitudinally through the manubrium and body.
Deep to the sternum the thymic remnant and fat lie in front of the pericardium.
The midline path keeps clear of the internal thoracic vessels, which lie lateral to the sternal edge, and of the pleural sacs.

blocks.answer: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, pectoral fascia and periosteum, sternum, thymic remnant and fat, pericardium.

blocks.markdown: **Thyroidectomy.** The thyroid lies in the front of the neck deep to the strap muscles (sternohyoid and sternothyroid), which are retracted or divided. The gland is supplied by the **superior thyroid artery** (from the external carotid) and the **inferior thyroid artery** (from the thyrocervical trunk). Structures at risk include: the **recurrent laryngeal nerve**, which runs in the groove between the trachea and oesophagus and passes close to the inferior thyroid artery, whose injury causes hoarseness; the **external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve**, which lies close to the superior thyroid artery and supplies cricothyroid; and the **parathyroid glands**, lying on the posterior surface of the thyroid, whose loss or devascularisation causes hypocalcaemia.

blocks.title: Predicting a complication
blocks.prompt: After a total thyroidectomy a patient has a hoarse voice and, 24 hours later, tingling around the mouth and cramps. Identify the structures involved.

steps.text: Hoarseness suggests injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which supplies most intrinsic laryngeal muscles.
Perioral tingling and cramps suggest a low calcium level.
The parathyroid glands lie on the posterior surface of the thyroid and may be removed or lose their blood supply, causing hypocalcaemia.
The two complications involve different structures that share the surgical field.

blocks.answer: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and parathyroid injury.

blocks.markdown: **Chest drain insertion and the safe triangle.** A drain is inserted through an intercostal space in the **safe triangle**, bounded by the anterior border of latissimus dorsi (posteriorly), the lateral border of pectoralis major (anteriorly) and a line at the level of the fifth intercostal space (inferiorly, roughly the level of the nipple in men), with the apex below the axilla. The drain is inserted in the fourth or fifth space, just above the upper border of the rib below, so the neurovascular bundle running under the rib above is avoided.

items: Posterior border: anterior edge of latissimus dorsi.
Anterior border: lateral edge of pectoralis major.
Inferior border: horizontal line at the level of the fifth intercostal space.

blocks.title: Why this triangle is safe
blocks.text: Within the triangle the chest wall is thin with few muscle layers, the internal thoracic vessels lie medially, and entry above the diaphragm and the fifth space keeps the needle clear of the liver and spleen.

blocks.title: Above the rib below
blocks.text: Needles and drains must pass over the upper border of the rib and not under the lower border of the rib above, where the intercostal vein, artery and nerve lie.

points: Thoracotomy crosses the muscles of the chest wall and intercostal muscles; the neurovascular bundle lies under the rib above, so incisions run along the rib below.
Median sternotomy splits the sternum, avoids the internal thoracic vessels and enters the pericardium.

Thyroidectomy endangers the recurrent laryngeal nerve, external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and parathyroids; the chest drain safe triangle uses latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major and the fifth space.

questions.stem: In which order do the intercostal vessels and nerve lie in the neurovascular bundle, from superior to inferior?

distractorRationale.c: The vein lies above the artery.
distractorRationale.d: The nerve lies below the artery.

questions.explanation: The mnemonic VAN gives the order from top to bottom in the subcostal groove. The vein is most exposed under the rib above.

questions.stem: A needle or drain is inserted into an intercostal space. Where should it pass to avoid the neurovascular bundle?

options.text: Just above the upper border of the rib below
Just below the lower border of the rib above
Through the middle of the rib

questions.correctOptionText: Just above the upper border of the rib below

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the bundle lies under the rib above, so stay on the upper border of the rib below.
distractorRationale.b: This is where the bundle runs.
distractorRationale.c: Needles do not pass through ribs.
distractorRationale.d: The sternum is midline, away from the intercostal space chosen.

questions.explanation: The bundle is protected by the subcostal groove on the underside of the upper rib. Passing over the top of the lower rib keeps the needle away from it.

questions.stem: During a median sternotomy, why is the incision kept strictly in the midline?

options.text: To avoid the internal thoracic vessels and pleura lying lateral to the sternum
To avoid the vagus nerve in the neck

questions.correctOptionText: To avoid the internal thoracic vessels and pleura lying lateral to the sternum

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the internal thoracic vessels run lateral to the sternal edge and the pleural sacs lie further lateral.
distractorRationale.b: The vagus nerve is in the neck and mediastinum, not at the sternal midline.

questions.explanation: Midline splitting avoids the internal thoracic vessels and pleura, which lie to the sides of the sternum.

questions.stem: What structure lies directly deep to the sternum and in front of the pericardium in the superior mediastinum of an adult?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the thymic remnant and fat lie behind the sternum.
distractorRationale.d: The thoracic duct lies posterior near the vertebral column.

questions.explanation: Behind the sternum, in front of the pericardium and great vessels, lie thymic remnant and fat. These are crossed after the sternum is divided.

questions.stem: A surgeon is ligating the inferior thyroid artery. Which nerve passes close to it and is at risk?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the recurrent laryngeal nerve is closely related to the inferior thyroid artery.
distractorRationale.b: The phrenic nerve lies on scalenus anterior.
distractorRationale.c: The hypoglossal nerve is higher in the neck.
distractorRationale.d: The long thoracic nerve is near the axilla.

questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove and is related to the inferior thyroid artery. Injury causes hoarseness.

questions.stem: After thyroid surgery a patient finds that she cannot reach high notes and her voice tires easily, but her voice is not hoarse. Which structure was most likely injured?

options.text: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

questions.correctOptionText: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it supplies cricothyroid, which tenses the vocal cords for pitch.
distractorRationale.b: Recurrent laryngeal injury typically causes hoarseness.
distractorRationale.d: Strap muscle division does not usually change pitch.

questions.explanation: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve lies near the superior thyroid artery and supplies cricothyroid. Loss reduces the ability to tense the vocal cords and raise pitch.

questions.stem: Which of the following forms the posterior border of the safe triangle for chest drain insertion?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: latissimus dorsi forms the posterior border.
distractorRationale.b: Pectoralis major forms the anterior border.
distractorRationale.c: The fifth intercostal space level forms the lower border.
distractorRationale.d: The mid-clavicular line is not a border of the triangle.

questions.explanation: The triangle is bounded by latissimus dorsi behind, pectoralis major in front and the fifth space below, with its apex below the axilla.

questions.stem: List the layers crossed in a thoracotomy in the fifth intercostal space and explain how the incision protects the neurovascular bundle.
markingGuide: External, internal and innermost intercostal muscles.
Bundle lies in the subcostal groove under the rib above, so pass along the upper border of the rib below.
questions.explanation: The bundle runs just below the rib above, so entry along the upper edge of the rib below stays clear of it.

questions.stem: Explain the anatomical basis of the safe triangle for chest drain insertion.
markingGuide: Borders: latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, fifth intercostal space; apex below axilla.
Thin chest wall with few muscle layers.
Avoids the internal thoracic vessels medially.
Fifth space avoids the diaphragm and upper abdominal organs below.
Insert above the upper border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
questions.explanation: The triangle keeps the drain in a thin part of the wall, away from muscle, breast, vessels and abdominal organs, and entry over the rib avoids the bundle.

questions.stem: A patient requires a thyroidectomy. Identify the structures at risk and explain the consequence of injury to each.
markingGuide: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve: loss of pitch (cricothyroid).
Superior and inferior thyroid arteries: bleeding.
Relationship of nerves to the arteries explains the risk.
questions.explanation: The nerves lie next to the thyroid vessels, and the parathyroids are on the posterior surface of the gland. Surgeons identify them to avoid injury.
